The default queue is Open with 2048 CPUs allocated — this is the total across the cluster. 100,000 CPU cores will never fit.

## Diagnosis Report

### Root Cause Origin
**Resource: Volcano Job `c091-vj`** — specifically the `jobs.batch.volcano.sh/c091-vj` resource in namespace `siclaw-eval-yye-20260602`.

### Root Cause Mechanism
The Volcano Job's container spec requests **`cpu: 100k`** (on both `limits.cpu` and `requests.cpu`). Kubernetes Quantity uses `k` as the **kilo** suffix (×1000), so:

| Value | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `100k` | **100,000** CPU cores |
| `100` | 100 CPU cores |
| `100m` | 0.1 CPU cores (100 millicores) |

No node in the cluster can satisfy 100,000 CPU cores — the largest real node has only **192** allocatable CPU cores (`gpu-10-208-55-159`, `hpe-node144`). The Volcano PodGroup's `minResources` mirrors this (`Cpu: 100k`), so the **conformance** plugin (first tier of the Volcano scheduler: `enqueue → allocate → preempt`) rejects the Job at enqueue time. No pods are ever created, zero events fire, and the Volcano Job and its PodGroup remain **Pending** permanently.

The `100k` was almost certainly intended as `100m` (100 millicores = 0.1 CPU) for a lightweight `busybox:1.36` container running `sleep 3600`.

### Evidence
1. **Volcano Job YAML** — `spec.tasks[0].template.spec.containers[0].resources.requests.cpu: 100k` and `limits.cpu: 100k`
   ```json
   {
     "limits": { "cpu": "100k", "memory": "64Mi" },
     "requests": { "cpu": "100k", "memory": "64Mi" }
   }
   ```
2. **PodGroup `minResources`** — `Cpu: 100k` echoed in `scheduling.volcano.sh/v1beta1`
3. **No pod exists** — `kubectl get pods -A | grep c091` returns nothing; the Volcano scheduler never dispatched the task
4. **No events** — `kubectl describe jobs.batch.volcano.sh c091-vj` shows `Events: <none>`; the Job has been Pending since creation (2d16h ago)
5. **Cluster capacity** — Largest real node: 192 CPUs; largest CPU-available node: 192 CPUs. Neither approaches 100,000.
6. **Volcano scheduler logs** — Silent on c091; the job never passed enqueue

### Impact Scope
- **Direct**: The Volcano Job `c091-vj` cannot run — it is permanently Pending (no pod scheduled in 2 days 16 hours)
- **Downstream**: None detected — no Services, Deployments, or other resources depend on c091

### Related but Separate Failures (not c091)
The namespace contains many other failures (image pull errors, crash loops, config errors, pending pods), but these are independent applications and do not cascade from c091.

### Confidence
**High** — the `cpu: 100k` request is definitively unschedulable. Kubernetes Quantity semantics (`k` = kilo = ×1000) are well-defined, the value appears verbatim in both the Volcano Job and PodGroup specs, and no node in the cluster has anywhere near 100k CPUs.

### Safe Remediation
**Fix the CPU quantity** in the Volcano Job `c091-vj` to use `100m` (100 millicores) instead of `100k` (100,000 cores):

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 64Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 64Mi
```

Then delete and recreate the Volcano Job (it does not support rolling updates):  
`kubectl delete jobs.batch.volcano.sh c091-vj -n siclaw-eval-yye-20260602` and re-apply the corrected YAML.

data:
  volcano-scheduler.conf: |
    actions: "enqueue, allocate, preempt"
    tiers:
    - plugins:
      - name: priority
        enablePreemptable: true
      - name: gang
        enablePreemptable: true
      - name: siquota
        enablePreemptable: true
      - name: conformance
    - plugins:
      - name: roce
      - name: predicates
        arguments:
          predicate.VolumeBindingEnable: false
      - name: gpuindex
      - name: nodeorder
      - name: binpack
        arguments:
          binpack.weight: 10
          binpack.cpu: 1
          binpack.memory: 5
          binpack.resources: nvidia.com/gpu
          binpack.resources.nvidia.com/gpu: 10
      - name: network-topology-aware
        arguments:
          weight: 20
          binpack.enabled: true
          binpack.proportion: 0.5
          binpack.cpu: 1
          binpack.memory: 2
          binpack.resources: nvidia.com/gpu
          binpack.resources.nvidia.com/gpu: 10

KIND:       Pod
VERSION:    v1

FIELD: limits <map[string]Quantity>


DESCRIPTION:
    Limits describes the maximum amount of compute resources allowed. More info:
    https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/
    Quantity is a fixed-point representation of a number. It provides convenient
    marshaling/unmarshaling in JSON and YAML, in addition to String() and
    AsInt64() accessors.
    
    The serialization format is:
    
    ``` <quantity>        ::= <signedNumber><suffix>
    
    	(Note that <suffix> may be empty, from the "" case in <decimalSI>.)
    
    <digit>           ::= 0 | 1 | ... | 9 <digits>          ::= <digit> |
    <digit><digits> <number>          ::= <digits> | <digits>.<digits> |
    <digits>. | .<digits> <sign>            ::= "+" | "-" <signedNumber>    ::=
    <number> | <sign><number> <suffix>          ::= <binarySI> |
    <decimalExponent> | <decimalSI> <binarySI>        ::= Ki | Mi | Gi | Ti | Pi
    | Ei
    
    	(International System of units; See:
    http://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Units/binary.html)
    
    <decimalSI>       ::= m | "" | k | M | G | T | P | E
    
    	(Note that 1024 = 1Ki but 1000 = 1k; I didn't choose the capitalization.)
    
    <decimalExponent> ::= "e" <signedNumber> | "E" <signedNumber> ```
    
    No matter which of the three exponent forms is used, no quantity may
    represent a number greater than 2^63-1 in magnitude, nor may it have more
    than 3 decimal places. Numbers larger or more precise will be capped or
    rounded up. (E.g.: 0.1m will rounded up to 1m.) This may be extended in the
    future if we require larger or smaller quantities.
    
    When a Quantity is parsed from a string, it will remember the type of suffix
    it had, and will use the same type again when it is serialized.
    
    Before serializing, Quantity will be put in "canonical form". This means
    that Exponent/suffix will be adjusted up or down (with a corresponding
    increase or decrease in Mantissa) such that:
    
    - No precision is lost - No fractional digits will be emitted - The exponent
    (or suffix) is as large as possible.
    
    The sign will be omitted unless the number is negative.
    
    Examples:
    
    - 1.5 will be serialized as "1500m" - 1.5Gi will be serialized as "1536Mi"
    
    Note that the quantity will NEVER be internally represented by a floating
    point number. That is the whole point of this exercise.
    
    Non-canonical values will still parse as long as they are well formed, but
    will be re-emitted in their canonical form. (So always use canonical form,
    or don't diff.)
    
    This format is intended to make it difficult to use these numbers without
    writing some sort of special handling code in the hopes that that will cause
    implementors to also use a fixed point implementation.

### Root Cause Mechanism
The Volcano Job's container spec requests **`cpu: 100k`** (on both `limits.cpu` and `requests.cpu`). Kubernetes Quantity uses `k` as the **kilo** suffix (×1000), so:

| Value | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `100k` | **100,000** CPU cores |
| `100` | 100 CPU cores |
| `100m` | 0.1 CPU cores (100 millicores) |

No node in the cluster can satisfy 100,000 CPU cores — the largest real node has only **192** allocatable CPU cores (`gpu-10-208-55-159`, `hpe-node144`). The Volcano PodGroup's `minResources` mirrors this (`Cpu: 100k`), so the **conformance** plugin (first tier of the Volcano scheduler: `enqueue → allocate → preempt`) rejects the Job at enqueue time. No pods are ever created, zero events fire, and the Volcano Job and its PodGroup remain **Pending** permanently.

The `100k` was almost certainly intended as `100m` (100 millicores = 0.1 CPU) for a lightweight `busybox:1.36` container running `sleep 3600`.
